row: | Zhu et al. (UIUC), [*JevAgentHarness: Benchmarking, Deploying and Training Decision Models That Share Control with LLMs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21412) (Oct 2026 ⚑) | Most loop steps end in a multiple-choice decision (tool, arguments, reflect, stop), which a small decision model can answer when its confidence clears a threshold fitted per decision point. The model most accurate on isolated questions solved only 69.5% of agent tasks, and delegating tool choice without a fitted threshold cost 19.0 points. With the cascade and a 4B model trained on the agent's own states, customer-service and household agents ran 81.1–89.0% cheaper and up to 2.5× faster within 3 points of success, on tasks like the training data; coding agents saved only 7.0–10.5% | [2610.21412](sources/zhu-2026-jevagentharness.pdf) | [02](notes/02-loop-shapes.md#the-canonical-skeleton) |

edits.old: JevAgentHarness (Zhu et al., 2026) counts **eight decision points** in one step of the loop and hands each to a small decision model that scores the listed options instead of generating text (one call cost 28% of an LLM call's time and 2.6% of its price):
edits.new: JevAgentHarness ([arXiv:2610.21412](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21412) (Zhu et al., 2026-10, preprint)) counts **eight decision points** in one step of the loop and hands each to a small decision model that scores the listed options instead of generating text (in one recorded episode, a call cost 28% of an LLM call's time and 2.6% of its price):
edits.why: Adds the arXiv cite (cited_in was empty because the note had no ID). The 28%/2.6% figure is from 'one recorded episode' (p. 2), not a general cost.

edits.old: With a threshold fitted per decision point (the *cascade*: decide when sure, defer to the LLM when not), agents ran **81–89% cheaper** and up to **2.5× faster** while losing less than 3 points of success.
edits.new: With a threshold fitted per decision point (the *cascade*: decide when sure, defer to the LLM when not) and a 4B decision model trained on the agent's own states, customer-service and household agents ran **81–89% cheaper** and up to **2.5× faster** on tasks like the training data, while losing less than 3 points of success. Coding agents, whose actions are free text, saved only 7–10.5%.
edits.why: Overstated: the 81.1-89.0% / 2.5x result needs the 4B models trained on each agent's states and holds on tasks like the training data, for customer-service and household agents (abstract; p. 3; Conclusion p. 8). With off-the-shelf JEV the chosen combination lost 2.2 points and failed non-inferiority (p. 8). Coding-agent savings 7.0-10.5% (Limitations, p. 8).

row: | Chen et al. (Mila, Google DeepMind), [*Are Self-Evolving Agents Continual Learners?*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.25858) (Oct 2026 ⚑) | ReasoningBank, GEPA and Meta-Harness on Gemini 3.6 Flash, over four drifting task streams built from BIRD, BFCL and ScienceWorld. Self-evolution lifts terminal accuracy on most streams (+1.4 to +3.7 points averaged over streams), but across the 12 method–stream pairs gains on the active task group come with losses on the others (r = −0.72). One base model | [2610.25858](sources/chen-2026-self-evolving-agents-continual-learners.pdf) | [08](notes/08-self-improving-loops.md#measuring-the-evolve-loop-itself) |

edits.old: **Plasticity costs stability.** Chen et al. (2026) ran three self-evolving methods (ReasoningBank memory retrieval, GEPA prompt evolution, Meta-Harness) on four task streams that drift in topic, workflow or domain. Self-evolution raised aggregate scores on most streams, but across all twelve runs the more a method learned on new tasks, the more it forgot on old ones (**r = −0.72**):
edits.new: **Plasticity costs stability.** Chen et al. ([arXiv:2610.25858](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.25858), 2026-10, preprint) ran three self-evolving methods (ReasoningBank memory retrieval, GEPA prompt evolution, Meta-Harness) with Gemini 3.6 Flash on four task streams, built from BIRD, BFCL and ScienceWorld, that drift in topic, workflow, domain or all three. Self-evolution raised aggregate scores on most streams, but across all twelve method–stream pairs the more a method gained on the task group it was training on, the more it lost on the others, both earlier groups (forgetting) and groups not yet seen (interference) (**r = −0.72**):
edits.why: Adds the arXiv cite and the setup (Gemini 3.6 Flash, BIRD/BFCL/ScienceWorld; p. 6). Stability S = -(interference + forgetting) (Table 1, Eq. 11), so 'forgot on old ones' understated it; the 4th stream is compound drift.

edits.old: and when two streams needed opposite workflows the agent rewrote its policy into its opposite.
edits.new: and when consecutive task groups in a stream needed opposite workflows the agent rewrote its policy into its opposite.
edits.why: The reversal happens between consecutive blocks within one stream (workflow drift and the BFCL transition of compound drift), not between two streams (p. 9, 'Behavioral reversal under conflicting workflows').
